reportSubtitle: Cost per inquiry nearly halved, and staffing now has its own page
summary:
Good cycle. Cost per inquiry came down from $383 to $214, which is the lowest it has been since May, and cost per click dropped to $5.31, the lowest since April. We also brought in 4 leads in 16 days, where the last cycle was 4 leads in 28 days.

The mobile bid reduction I made last cycle was doing what I hoped, but we're going to scrap it in favor of switching back to automated bidding.

I met with the google ads rep today and he basically confirmed all of my suspcisions on why performance went down in spring. Switched back on the AI, and as a bonus I created a new funnel page for the staffing page. More details below.

metrics.label: Ad spend (16 days)
metrics.note: About $53 a day, just inside the $60 daily budget.

metrics.label: Inquiries
metrics.note: Four in sixteen days. Last cycle took twenty eight days for the same number.

funnel.title: Ad to inquiry funnel (Aug 25 - Sep 9)
funnel.notes: Fewer clicks than last cycle but the same number of inquiries, on roughly half the spend. Each click is both cheaper and more likely to enquire.

data.note: Cost per inquiry has come down two cycles running, from $560 to $383 to $214. Cost per click fell at the same time, which is the clearest sign the budget is reaching better-matched searches.

charts.title: Where this cycle's four inquiries came from

data.note: 'Event bartending service' improved from $296 per inquiry last cycle to $169 this cycle on the same search. 'Mobile bar Denver' produced an inquiry for $42, the second cheapest this account has recorded.

charts.title: The two services now have their own pages

rows: Hourly rates, what's included, how many bartenders they need
Bar catering, mobile bar, full service
Packages from $800, custom menu, full setup
data.note: Previously both searches landed on general pages that covered everything. Someone comparing hourly bartender rates had to hunt for a number, and a lot of them left instead. Each page now answers the question that brought the person there.

findings.title: Cost per inquiry has halved twice in a row
findings.description: It went from $560 in early summer to $383 last cycle to $214 this cycle. Cost per click fell alongside it, from $6.74 to $5.31, which is the lowest since April. The two moving together means we are winning cheaper auctions on searches that still convert, rather than simply buying less traffic.

findings.title: Inquiries are arriving at nearly double the rate
findings.description: Four inquiries in sixteen days works out to about 1.75 a week, against roughly one a week last cycle. Same daily budget, more inquiries per dollar.

findings.title: Two keywords produced everything again, and both got cheaper
findings.description: 'Event bartending service' delivered three inquiries at $169 each, improved from $296 last cycle. 'Mobile bar Denver' delivered one at $42. The remaining searches spent $306 without producing an inquiry, which is normal at this volume and not yet enough evidence to cut anything.

actions.title: Built a dedicated staffing page
actions.description: People searching for bartenders to hire now land on a page written for exactly that: hourly rates up front, what each person brings, certification and insurance, and guidance on how many bartenders an event of their size needs.

actions.title: Matched each ad to the right page
actions.description: Staffing searches go to the staffing page, full bar service searches go to the packages page. Same budget, but people now arrive somewhere that answers what they actually typed into Google.

actions.title: Moved bidding to Google's automated system
actions.description: Google's system historically produced this account's best results but struggled during peak season when competition pushed prices up. With competition easing into autumn and a larger budget than it had last spring, this is the right window to give it back.

actions.title: Tuned the booking pages for speed and brand consistency
actions.description: Faster loading on phones and colours matched to your main site, so the ad pages feel like part of the same business rather than a separate thing.

recommendation.title: Let the new pages and automated bidding settle, then read the results properly
recommendation.context: Three things changed this cycle: the staffing page, the page each ad points to, and the bidding system. All of them need a couple of weeks before the numbers mean anything. Google's automated bidding in particular goes through a learning period where results move around before they settle, so I expect some week-to-week noise that is not signal.

changes.title: No further changes for two to three weeks
changes.description: Budget stays at $60 a day and the keyword list stays as it is. I will keep reviewing incoming searches and blocking anything clearly off target, which does not disturb the test.
changes.impact: A clean read on whether the separate pages convert better than the general ones did, and whether automated bidding beats manual on this account.

changes.title: Then split the two services into separate campaigns groups
changes.description: Staffing keywords and bar service keywords currently share one pool and compete with each other. Separating them lets each set its own bids and makes the ads more closely matched to the searches, which Google rewards with lower prices.
changes.impact: Lower cost per click on both sides, and the ability to see which service is actually driving the business.

nextSteps: Let the new staffing page and the automated bidding run undisturbed and measure the effect.
Continue reviewing incoming searches and blocking any that are clearly off target.
Watch whether the autumn easing in competition continues to bring cost per click down.
Report back in late September with the new pages measured and a recommendation on splitting the two services.
